items.readable_text:
Content:
Given the scalar [MATH: a,] the multiplicative inverse of [MATH: a] is defined as the scalar [MATH: a^{-1}] such that
[MATH: a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1.]

Content:
For example, the multiplicative inverse of [MATH: 2] is the number [MATH: 2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}] because

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = 2\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 1.]

Content:
Similarly, given a square [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] the inverse of [MATH: A] is defined as the [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A^{-1}] such that
[MATH: A \cdot A^{-1} = A^{-1} \cdot A = I_n,]
where [MATH: I_n] is the [MATH: n\times n] identity matrix.

Content:
For example, suppose we're given the following [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix:
[MATH: [− 1|− 1; 1|2]]

Content:
The inverse of the above matrix is given by

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|− 1; 1|1]]

Content:
To verify that the above matrix is in fact the inverse of [MATH: A,] first observe that if we multiply [MATH: A] by the above matrix [MATH: A^{-1},] then we get the identity matrix [MATH: I_2\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [− 1|− 1; 1|2]_(⏟)_(A)[− 2|− 1; 1|1]_(⏟)_(A^{− 1})|= [− 1 ⋅ (− 2) + (− 1) ⋅ 1|− 1 ⋅ (− 1) + (− 1) ⋅ 1; 1 ⋅ (− 2) + 2 ⋅ 1|1 ⋅ (− 1) + 2 ⋅ 1]; = [1|0; 0|1]; = I_{2}✓]

Content:
Likewise, if we multiply [MATH: A^{-1}] by [MATH: A,] then we also get the identity matrix [MATH: I_2\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|− 1; 1|1][− 1|− 1; 1|2]_(⏟)_(A)|= I_{2}✓]

Content:
We do not yet know how to find the inverse of a matrix. However, we can verify that one matrix is the inverse of the other by carrying out the same procedure as we did here.
